review.notes: Built on the course: SIPOC, VSM, value-added, Little's Law, PCE, TIMWOODS, 5S, takt, standard work, operators needed, visual management, kanban, PDCA, Pareto, fishbone. Calculations checked. Fictional company.

content.company: Clearwater Bottling (fictional), a water and soft drinks plant with two lines
content.briefing: Line 2 misses daily output, orders wait for days, and the floor is cluttered. The plant manager gives you 8 weeks to improve flow and quality without new machines.

variants.text: You start mapping line 2 on one page: suppliers, inputs, 5 main steps, outputs and customers. What tool is this?

choices.f: A one-page, high-level view with a fixed start and end.
That finds causes of one problem.
That ranks causes by size.

variants.text: Which step is value-added for the customer?

choices.f: It changes the product, the customer would pay for it, done right first time.

choices.t: Moving pallets to a storage area
choices.f: Transport adds no value the customer pays for.
Over-processing, unless the customer requires it.

variants.text: 600 orders are in process and the plant completes 150 a day. What is the lead time?

choices.f: Little's Law: WIP / completion rate. Cut WIP to cut lead time.
That is the completion rate, not lead time.
You divided the wrong way.

variants.text: Value-added time is 2 hours. Total lead time is 40 hours. What is process cycle efficiency?

choices.f: Correct: 2 / 40. Most of the time is waiting.
That is 40 / 2 divided by 100. Use 2 / 40.
That is the non-value-added share.

variants.text: Line 2 fills 2,000 extra bottles a day 'to stay busy'. They sit in the warehouse for weeks. Which waste?

choices.f: The worst waste: it creates inventory, transport and handling.
Motion is people moving more than needed.
Here the line keeps running, not waiting.

variants.text: Operators walk 40 metres to fetch caps every 20 minutes. Which waste?

choices.f: Unnecessary movement of people. Caps go to the point of use.
No bad product is made.
Nothing extra is done to the product.

variants.text: The line has old tools, broken parts and unused boxes everywhere. Which 5S step first?

choices.t: Sort: red-tag what is not needed
choices.f: Remove everything not needed before arranging anything.
Cleaning clutter you do not need wastes effort.
First remove, then arrange, clean and standardise.

variants.text: After 5S, the area slides back within a month. What was missing?

choices.t: Sustain: regular audits led by leaders
choices.f: Leaders check weekly and display the score.
Materials do not keep habits.
Space fills up again without discipline.

variants.text: Available time: 27,000 seconds per shift. Customer demand: 900 cases per shift. What is takt time?

choices.f: Correct: 27,000 / 900. The line must produce one case every 30 s.
That is the demand, not the pace.
You divided the wrong way.

variants.text: Total work content is 150 seconds per case. Takt time is 30 seconds. How many operators?

choices.f: Correct: 150 / 30. Then balance the work across them.
150 / 30 is exactly 5. Round up only when there is a remainder.
That is the takt time.

variants.text: Work content is 140 seconds; takt is 30 seconds. How many operators?

choices.f: 140 / 30 = 4.67, rounded up to 5.
4 people cannot meet takt. The line falls behind.
Round up whole operators, then balance.

variants.text: Cap stock runs out without warning, stopping the line.

choices.t: Kanban with min and max lines
choices.f: An empty bin or card signals replenishment in time.
Overproduction and inventory waste.

choices.t: Ask the operator to watch it
choices.f: A visual signal works better than memory.

variants.text: Supervisors cannot tell if the line is ahead or behind until the shift ends.

choices.f: Status visible at a glance in seconds; problems are fixed in the hour.

choices.t: A daily email with output totals
choices.f: Too late to act during the shift.
Helpful, but a visual board shows it without asking.

variants.text: Who should write the standard work for the filling station?

choices.t: The people who do the work, with the lead
choices.f: They know the details, and they follow what they helped write.

choices.t: An engineer, alone, at head office
choices.f: Standards written far from the work are often ignored.
A manual is not your sequence, takt and WIP.

variants.text: Rejects by cause this month: label crooked 120, cap loose 60, short fill 15, other 5. Where do you start?

choices.f: Pareto: a few causes create most of the problem. 120 of 200.

choices.t: Short fill: it sounds most serious
choices.f: Start with the biggest impact first.
Spreading effort fixes nothing fully.

variants.text: You list causes of crooked labels under Man, Machine, Method, Material, Measurement and Environment. What tool?

choices.f: It organises possible causes before you test them.
That maps flow, not causes of a defect.
That gives a high-level process view.

variants.text: You think a new label guide will fix crooked labels. How do you introduce it?

choices.t: PDCA: test on one shift, measure, then act
choices.f: Rejects fall 70% on the test shift. You standardise it.

choices.t: Install it on both lines at once
choices.f: If it fails, both lines fail.

choices.t: Wait for a perfect design first
choices.f: Small tests teach faster than waiting.

variants.text: The test worked. What does 'Act' in PDCA mean now?

choices.t: Standardise it in the standard work
choices.f: Make the improvement the new standard so it lasts.
Without standardising, the gain fades.

choices.t: Repeat the test for a year
choices.f: Once proven, standardise and move on.

variants.text: An experienced operator has ideas to cut changeover time, but nobody asks him. Which waste?

choices.f: The eighth waste: people's ideas and talent left unused.
Not about idle time here.
Not about moving materials.

variants.text: Bottles are moved three times between filling and the truck. Which waste?

choices.f: Unnecessary movement of materials. You redesign the layout.
Motion is people; transport is materials.
That is about making too much.
